docs.title: ewe: Ecopath with Ecosim for Python and R
docs.text:
ewe runs Ecopath with Ecosim (EwE) models from Python and R, on macOS, Linux and Windows. It drives the same computational core as the EwE desktop application (EwECore), so the numbers are EwE's own.

import ewe

m = ewe.library.load("tampa-bay")            # or ewe.open("my_model.eiixml" / "my_model.ewemdb")
m.ecopath().diagnostics                       # balance check: TL, B, P/B, Q/B, EE, mortalities
sim = m.ecosim(years=30, effort={"Bait Trawl": 0.5})
sim.biomass                                   # pandas DataFrame: time x group
sim.plot()                                    # matplotlib chart
m.save("tampa_edited.ewemdb")                 # opens in EwE on Windows

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
Run Ecopath mass balance, Ecosim scenarios with effort and vulnerability overrides, Ecospace, Ecotracer Build and edit Create models from scratch or edit existing ones: groups, diets, fleets, catch, stanzas, Ecosim scenarios, time series Fit and test Fit to time series (vulnerabilities, primary production anomaly), Monte Carlo Manage Management Strategy Evaluation, MSY and FMSY, fishing policy search Analyse Network analysis (mixed trophic impacts, keystoneness, ascendency), ecological indicators Plot A chart for every result, with matplotlib (Python) or ggplot2 (R) Exchange Read and write EwE's Access databases (.ewemdb) on any OS; .eiixml everywhere

Results come back as pandas DataFrames in Python and data frames in R. The two packages have the same calls (m.ecosim(...) in Python is ewe_ecosim(m, ...) in R) and return the same numbers.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
• Install: one pip install; the wheels include everything (no .NET, Java or Access driver).
  • Python quickstart or the R guide.
  • Try it in Google Colab: ewe_colab_quickstart.ipynb, or build a model from scratch with ewe_colab_broughton_herring.ipynb (a 1975 Broughton Archipelago herring model: stanzas, balancing, Ecosim scenarios and a fit to the DFO spawn index).

Prototype

Version 0.1.1 is a prototype. The API can still change, and results should be checked against the EwE desktop application for work that matters. See About for what is tested where.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
Python (ewe)          R (ewe)            other tools
      \                  |                   /
       JSON lines over stdio (one engine process per model)
                          |
                    ewe-engine  ── EwECore + EwEUtils (EwE's own core, .NET 10)
                    ewe-access  ── Jackcess via IKVM (Access files on any OS)

ewe-engine adds a small API on top of EwE's core without changing the science code. The wheels and R bundles ship it self-contained, with the .NET runtime included.

docs.title: What is tested where
docs.text:
macOS arm64 macOS x64 Linux x64 Linux arm64 Windows x64 Core, engine, Python and R test suites (from source) yes yes yes Installed wheel, every SDK call on every library model yes yes (Rosetta) Colab not yet not yet Access files opened by EwE's own reader yes

Results are compared with stored reference outputs for every library model, and the Python and R packages are checked against each other. Reference outputs come from this engine, not from the EwE 6.7 desktop release; agreement with the desktop application on your own models is worth checking.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Prototype: names and options can still change before 1.0.
  • EwE plug-ins other than Network Analysis and Ecological Indicators are not exposed.
  • The inprocess (pythonnet) backend needs a .NET 10 runtime installed separately.

docs.title: Access files (.ewemdb)
docs.text:
The EwE desktop application stores models as Microsoft Access databases (.ewemdb, .mdb). Microsoft only provides Access drivers for Windows, so ewe brings its own converter, ewe-access, which reads and writes these files on macOS and Linux too. It is included in the wheels and R bundles: nothing else to install.

m = ewe.open("Georgia_Strait.EwEmdb")     # read: converted to .eiixml on the fly off Windows
m.save("my_model.ewemdb")                 # write: opens in EwE on Windows
doc.save("new_model.ewemdb")              # a model built with a ModelDocument

from ewe.convert import mdb_to_eiixml, eiixml_to_mdb
mdb_to_eiixml("model.ewemdb", "model.eiixml")
eiixml_to_mdb("model.eiixml", "model.ewemdb")

m <- ewe_open("Georgia_Strait.EwEmdb")
ewe_save(m, "my_model.ewemdb")
ewe_to_ewemdb("model.eiixml", "model.ewemdb"); ewe_from_ewemdb("model.ewemdb", "model.eiixml")

Command line: ewe-access to-ewemdb model.eiixml model.ewemdb and ewe-access to-eiixml model.ewemdb model.eiixml.

docs.title: How it works and how it is checked
docs.text:
• ewe-access uses Jackcess (Apache 2.0), compiled to .NET with IKVM, so no Java runtime is needed.
  • New databases start from EwE6.mdb, the empty model EwE itself creates new models from, so the tables, column types, relationships and schema version are exactly what EwE expects. Tables the template does not have (for example plug-in data) are added, so nothing is lost.
  • Blank values stay blank (NULL): EwE applies its own defaults to them, which can differ from the Access column defaults.
  • Tested on Windows with Microsoft's Access Database Engine: every library model written by ewe-access opens in EwE's own Access reader with identical Ecopath and Ecosim results.

docs.title: Opening .eiixml in the EwE desktop app
docs.text: EwE's desktop application can open .eiixml files read-only. Builds of EwE from this repository also offer to import an .eiixml into a new, editable model database when you open one (File > Open), using EwE's own import framework. That path is tested the same way: the imported database gives identical results to the .eiixml.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Each wheel bundles the EwE engine, the Access converter and the .NET runtime, plus the model library. Nothing else needs installing: no .NET, Java or Microsoft Access driver. Python 3.10 or newer.

Platform Install macOS 15+, Apple silicon pip install https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-0.1.1-py3-none-macosx_15_0_arm64.whl macOS 15+, Intel pip install https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-0.1.1-py3-none-macosx_15_0_x86_64.whl Linux x86-64 (glibc 2.28+, incl. Google Colab) pip install https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-0.1.1-py3-none-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl Linux arm64 pip install https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-0.1.1-py3-none-manylinux_2_28_aarch64.whl Windows x64 pip install https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-0.1.1-py3-none-win_amd64.whl

Charts need matplotlib: pip install matplotlib (or "ewe[plot] @ <wheel URL>").

A wheel is about 65 MB to download and 170 MB installed; most of that is the .NET runtime and the Java class library used for Access files. Checksums: SHA256SUMS.txt.

Apple silicon

Use an arm64 Python (for example /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.13 -m venv .venv). Some tools pick an Intel Python, which then rejects the arm64 wheel with "is not a supported wheel on this platform".

Check the install:

import ewe
print(ewe.find_engine())              # .../site-packages/ewe/bin/ewe-engine
print(ewe.library.list())             # the bundled model library

docs.title: R
docs.text:
The R package talks to the same engine. Install the package, then the engine bundle for your platform:

install.packages(c("jsonlite", "processx"))
install.packages("https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe_0.1.1.tar.gz", repos = NULL, type = "source")

library(ewe)
ewe_install_engine("https://github.com/dexterfichuk/ewe-wheels/releases/download/v0.1.1/ewe-bundle-osx-arm64.tar.gz")   # once per machine
m <- ewe_library_load("tampa-bay")

Bundles: osx-arm64 · osx-x64 · linux-x64 · linux-arm64 · win-x64. ewe_install_engine() also takes a downloaded archive or an unpacked folder. Charts need ggplot2.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
With the .NET 10 SDK:

dotnet build Sources/EwEEngine -c Release
dotnet build Sources/EwEAccess -c Release        # Access files (.ewemdb)
pip install -e "python[test,plot]"
pytest python

The engine is found through EWE_ENGINE, a bundle inside the package, or a build in the source tree; the Access converter through EWE_ACCESS. Build wheels with python python/tools/build_wheel.py <rid> (osx-arm64, osx-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, win-x64), which also writes the R bundles.

docs.title: Network analysis and ecological indicators
docs.text:
na = m.network_analysis()                  # EwE's Network Analysis plug-in, on the Ecopath model
na.stats                                   # throughput, Finn's cycling index, ascendency, TE, ...
na.groups                                  # keystoneness, PPR, L index, ascendency by group
na.mti_matrix()                            # mixed trophic impacts (rows impact columns)
m.ecosim_network_analysis(years=20).annual()   # network indices per Ecosim time step

ind = m.indicators(ecosim=True)            # Ecological Indicators plug-in
ind.values                                 # Ecopath values by indicator code (TotalB, TLC, MTI, ...)
ind.ecosim                                 # time step x indicator
ind.catalog                                # names, descriptions and units

Both run EwE's own plug-ins (Network Analysis and Ecological Indicators) on the loaded model.

docs.title: Ecopath
docs.text:
path = m.ecopath()
path.balanced                 # True when every living group has EE <= 1
path.unbalanced_groups        # groups with EE > 1
path.groups                   # full outputs per group
path.diagnostics              # the columns used when balancing: type, tl, biomass, pb, qb, ee, ge, f, m2, m0

inputs = m.ecopath_inputs()
inputs.groups                 # B, P/B, Q/B, EE, ... as entered (NaN where left blank)
inputs.diet_matrix            # prey x predator
inputs.catch                  # landings and discards by fleet and group

When Ecopath does not balance, unbalanced_groups lists the groups with EE above 1, and diagnostics shows each group's ee and m2 (predation mortality): lower the predators' consumption of that group, raise its biomass or P/B, or move some diet to import.

docs.title: Ecosim
docs.text:
sim = m.ecosim()                                   # first scenario, its own settings
sim = m.ecosim(scenario="all fit", years=50)       # by name or 1-based index
sim = m.ecosim(effort={"Trawl": 0.5, "Seine": 2})  # multiply a fleet's whole effort series
sim = m.ecosim(vulnerability_multiplier=2)         # scale every predator-prey vulnerability

sim.groups        # long table: step, time, group, biomass, catch, f, z, m2, qb, tl, value
sim.fleets        # long table: step, time, fleet, group, catch, landings, f, value
sim.summary       # start and end biomass per group
sim.biomass       # time x group (wide); also sim.catch, sim.relative_biomass, sim.wide("f")
sim.messages      # warnings from the run, e.g. groups starting far from their Ecopath biomass

Ecosim steps are monthly. The scenario is reloaded for every run, so overrides never leak into the next call. To change a scenario permanently (effort series, vulnerabilities, forcing), edit the model's document and save it.

docs.title: Building and editing models
docs.text:
Models are edited as a ModelDocument: a plain, JSON-serialisable description of the model (groups, diet, fleets, catch, stanzas, Ecosim scenarios, time series). Edit it, check it, run it without saving, or save it as .eiixml or .ewemdb.

import ewe

doc = ewe.new_model("Toy bay", area=100)
doc.add_group("Fish", biomass_area=2, pb=0.8, qb=4)
doc.add_group("Zooplankton", pb=30, qb=100, ee=0.9)    # B is estimated
doc.add_group("Phytoplankton", "producer", biomass_area=15, pb=120)
doc.add_group("Detritus", "detritus", biomass_area=50)  # becomes everyone's detritus fate
doc.set_diet("Fish", {"Zooplankton": 1})
doc.set_diet("Zooplankton", {"Phytoplankton": 0.8, "Detritus": 0.2})
doc.add_fleet("Trawl")
doc.set_catch("Trawl", "Fish", landings=0.3)
doc.add_ecosim_scenario("Baseline", years=20)
print(doc.validate())
with doc.open() as m:            # run without saving
    m.ecopath().diagnostics
doc.save("toy.eiixml")

m = ewe.open("Tampa_Bay.eiixml")
doc = m.document()               # groups, diet, fleets, catch, stanzas, scenarios
doc.set_group("Pin Fish", pb=2.5)
doc.remove_group("Catfish")      # cleans diets, catch and its Ecosim/Ecospace data
m.apply(doc)                     # the session now runs the edit; the file is untouched
m.save("Tampa_Bay_edited.eiixml")

doc.groups, doc.diet, doc.diet_matrix, doc.catch, ... are DataFrame views; update_groups, set_diet_matrix and set_catch_table take DataFrames back. doc.diet_matrix is prey (rows) by predator (columns). None means "not entered". Documents are plain JSON (doc.to_json(), ewe.load_document()), described by ewe.model_schema(). Invalid documents raise ewe.ModelValidationError with an errors list.

Field notes:

  • Units: ewe.new_model("Bay", unit_currency="wet_weight", unit_time="year") (names in ewe.authoring.UNIT_CURRENCY and UNIT_TIME; EwE's integer codes also work).
  • diet_import on a group is the share of its diet eaten outside the model; the diet proportions plus diet_import should sum to 1.
  • When Ecopath does not balance, m.ecopath().unbalanced_groups lists groups with EE above 1, and diagnostics has each group's ee and m2 (predation mortality): lower the predators' consumption of that group, raise its B or P/B, or move some diet to diet_import.

docs.title: Multi-stanza groups
docs.text:
doc.add_group("Herring adult", biomass_area=3.3, pb=0.7, qb=6.3, vbk=0.48)
doc.add_group("Herring juvenile", pb=1.5)           # B and Q/B come from the stanza calculation
doc.add_stanza("Herring", [("Herring juvenile", 0, 1.5), ("Herring adult", 24, 0.7)], wmat_winf=0.35)
doc.calculate_stanzas()                             # fills the juvenile's B and Q/B (after the diets are set)

Life stages are (group, age_start_months, Z), youngest first. leading_stage and leading_cb (1-based, default the oldest stage) name the stage whose B and Q/B you enter; calculate_stanzas() derives the others the way the desktop app does. It loads the whole model, so call it once every group has a diet. Every life stage shares one von Bertalanffy K (vbk): validate() rejects a stanza without one and gives stages left blank the others' K. The stage's mortality is the Z the stanza calculation uses; keep each group's pb equal to it. spawn_prop is the fraction of a stage that spawns (1 when left out; only weight above wmat_winf makes eggs).

docs.title: Ecosim inputs and time series
docs.text:
doc.add_ecosim_scenario("1975-2025", years=50)
doc.set_effort("1975-2025", "Roe herring", [1] * 5 + [2] * 10 + [1])   # per year; the last value holds
doc.set_vulnerabilities("1975-2025", {("Seals", "Herring adult"): 5})  # or a DataFrame, or one number
doc.add_time_series("Surveys", "Spawn index", "biomass_relative", index_by_year,
                    group="Herring adult", first_year=1975)            # None where there is no data
doc.save("herring.eiixml")

m = ewe.open("herring.eiixml")
fit = m.fit(dataset="Surveys")       # fit vulnerabilities to the spawn index

Effort is relative to the Ecopath (base) effort. A fleet's effort or a dataset in the document replaces the stored one of the same name on save; others stay as they are. Time series types: ewe.ModelDocument.TIME_SERIES_TYPES (biomass_relative, biomass_absolute, catches, fishing_effort per fleet, fishing_mortality, ...). m.ecosim().messages lists warnings from a run, such as groups that start far from their Ecopath biomass.

The document format is described by a JSON Schema: ewe.model_schema(). See the ModelDocument reference for every method.

docs.title: Management: MSE, MSY, FMSY and policy search
docs.text:
Management tools take EwE's settings by name and return the settings they used:

mse = m.mse(trials=50, seed=1,                         # Management Strategy Evaluation
            parameters={"regulatory_mode": "UseRegulations"},
            groups={"Anchovy": {"fixed_f": 0.3}},
            fleets={"Seiners": {"quota_type": "Weakest"}})
mse.groups                                 # biomass/catch statistics and % below/above limits
mse.wide("biomass", "q05")                 # yearly 5th percentile per group

msy = m.msy("Anchovy")                     # equilibrium yield curve of one group (or mode="fleet")
msy.yield_curve(), msy.optimum
m.fmsy().groups                            # FMSY and MSY of every fished group

ps = m.policy_search(weights={"economic_weight": 1, "ecosystem_weight": 0.5}, max_evaluations=200)
ps.result, ps.multipliers                  # objective and the effort multiplier per fleet

R has the same calls: ewe_mse(), ewe_msy(), ewe_fmsy(), ewe_policy_search().

Settings are EwE's own, by name; each result also returns the settings the run used.

docs.title: Opening models
docs.text:
m = ewe.open("Tampa_Bay.eiixml")        # EwE XML export, any OS
m = ewe.open("Georgia_Strait.EwEmdb")   # EwE Access database, any OS
m = ewe.library.load("anchovy-bay")     # the bundled model library

.ewemdb/.mdb files are read on Windows by EwE itself and elsewhere through the bundled Access converter (see Access files). ewe.open() also takes a ModelDocument to run a model without saving it first.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
m.save("copy.eiixml")                   # the session continues on the saved file
m.save("copy.ewemdb")                   # EwE Access database for the desktop app

docs.title: Model library
docs.text:
The wheels include a small library of models that load in one line and double as the regression tests' reference cases:

ewe.library.list()          # id, name, groups, fleets, scenarios, source, licence
ewe.library.card("tampa-bay")
m = ewe.library.load("georgia-strait")
ewe.library.golden("anchovy-bay")       # reference outputs used by the tests
id model groups fleets Ecosim scenarios anchovy-bay Anchovy Bay (teaching model) 11 5 1 generic-37 Generic marine ecosystem 37 1 1 georgia-strait Strait of Georgia, BC 27 4 3 georgia-strait-discards Strait of Georgia, discards variant 27 4 3 tampa-bay Tampa Bay, Florida 52 7 1

All are distributed with the EwE source under the EUPL-1.2.

docs.title: Engine processes
docs.text: backend="process" (the default) runs the engine as a child process per model and talks to it over a JSON protocol. EwE's core keeps process-wide state, so separate processes are what makes several open models (and parallel runs) safe. backend="inprocess" loads the engine into Python with pythonnet; it needs a .NET 10 runtime on the machine and handles one model at a time.

docs.title: Time series, fitting, Monte Carlo, Ecospace, Ecotracer
docs.text:
m = ewe.library.load("anchovy-bay")
m.time_series().datasets                   # time series datasets in the model
fit = m.fit(dataset=1)                     # fit to time series (vulnerability search)
fit.ss_before, fit.ss_after, fit.changed   # changed vulnerabilities per feeding link
pp = m.fit(dataset=1, anomaly_spline_points=5)   # also a primary production anomaly
pp.anomaly                                 # month, year, value (multiplier on production)
m.save_fit(pp, "fitted.eiixml")            # store vulnerabilities + anomaly in the model
m.apply_fit(pp)                            # or only use them in this session

mc = m.monte_carlo(trials=100, seed=1)     # resample Ecopath inputs, rerun Ecosim
mc.quantiles()                             # 5/50/95% of end/start biomass per group

sp = m.ecospace(years=5)                   # Ecospace
sp.wide("biomass")                         # time x group, totals over the map
sp.biomass_maps["Cod"]                     # final rows x cols array, NaN on land
sp.messages                                # warnings the core raised (pop-ups in the desktop app)

ewe.open("model_with_tracer.eiixml").ecotracer(years=10).wide()   # contaminant concentrations

Management tools take EwE's settings by name and return the settings they used:

mse = m.mse(trials=50, seed=1,                         # Management Strategy Evaluation
            parameters={"regulatory_mode": "UseRegulations"},
            groups={"Anchovy": {"fixed_f": 0.3}},
            fleets={"Seiners": {"quota_type": "Weakest"}})
mse.groups                                 # biomass/catch statistics and % below/above limits
mse.wide("biomass", "q05")                 # yearly 5th percentile per group

msy = m.msy("Anchovy")                     # equilibrium yield curve of one group (or mode="fleet")
msy.yield_curve(), msy.optimum
m.fmsy().groups                            # FMSY and MSY of every fished group

ps = m.policy_search(weights={"economic_weight": 1, "ecosystem_weight": 0.5}, max_evaluations=200)
ps.result, ps.multipliers                  # objective and the effort multiplier per fleet

R has the same calls: ewe_mse(), ewe_msy(), ewe_fmsy(), ewe_policy_search().

Nothing these runs change (fitted vulnerabilities, Monte Carlo samples) carries over to the next call. Keep a fit with save_fit (writes the vulnerabilities where the EwE desktop app keeps them, and the anomaly as a forcing function "PP anomaly (fit)" applied to the production rate of every producer) or apply_fit. A saved fit reloads with the ss_after the fit reported. fit starts from the scenario's own vulnerabilities and keeps the best values the search tried; reset_vulnerabilities=True starts from EwE's default of 2 instead, like the desktop app's "Use default v" option.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
Charts need matplotlib: pip install "ewe[plot]". Every result has a plot accessor that draws the usual chart from the DataFrames it holds, and returns the matplotlib Axes (an array of Axes for small multiples) to restyle or save:

sim = m.ecosim()
sim.plot()                                  # biomass, one line per group (yearly means)
sim.plot.biomass(relative=True, groups=["Cod", "Anchovy"])
sim.plot.catch(); sim.plot.variable("f")
sim.plot.fleets()                           # landings by fleet, stacked
sim.plot.compare({"seiners x2": m.ecosim(effort={"Seiners": 2})}, label="baseline")

ts = m.time_series(2)
ts.plot.fit({"before": sim, "after": after})   # observed vs predicted, relative series scaled as EwE does
m.fit(2).plot()                             # SS by iteration; .plot.vulnerabilities()
m.monte_carlo(trials=50).plot()             # end/start biomass across trials: median and 5-95%
m.mse(trials=10).plot("catch")              # yearly median and 5-95% band
m.msy("Anchovy").plot()                     # catch and biomass against F, base F and optimum marked
m.fmsy().plot()                             # base F against FMSY per group
sp = m.ecospace()
sp.plot.map("Cod"); sp.plot.maps()          # final biomass maps; sp.plot() for totals over time
m.plot.foodweb()                            # flow diagram: trophic level, biomass, consumption links
m.ecopath().plot()                          # biomass against trophic level
m.network_analysis().plot()                 # mixed trophic impacts heatmap

ewe.plot.set_theme("dark")                  # dark palette for every chart after this

More than eight series never share one set of axes: they become small multiples, or (stacked fleets) the smallest fold into "Other". The functions behind the accessors are in ewe.plot (ewe.plot.ecosim(sim, ...), ewe.plot.compare(...), ewe.plot.fit(...)).

See ewe.plot for every chart function and its options.

docs.title: Python quickstart
docs.text:
import ewe

m = ewe.library.load("tampa-bay")       # a model from the bundled library
m                                       # <ewe.Model 'Tampa Bay': 52 groups, 7 fleets, 1 Ecosim scenarios>
m.groups, m.fleets, m.scenarios         # what is in it

path = m.ecopath()                      # mass balance
path.balanced, path.unbalanced_groups
path.diagnostics                        # tl, biomass, pb, qb, ee, ge, f, m2, m0 per group

sim = m.ecosim(years=30, effort={"Bait Trawl": 0.5})   # halve one fleet's effort
sim.biomass                             # time x group
sim.catch
sim.fleets.groupby("fleet").catch.sum()

sim.plot()                              # needs matplotlib
m.save("tampa_bay_copy.ewemdb")         # an EwE Access database, opens in EwE on Windows
m.close()

Every model runs in its own engine process; with ewe.open(...) as m: closes it for you. Overrides such as years, effort and vulnerability_multiplier apply to that one run only.

docs.title: R guide
docs.text:
library(ewe)
m <- ewe_library_load("tampa-bay")         # or ewe_open("my_model.eiixml" / "my_model.ewemdb")
path <- ewe_ecopath(m)
subset(path$groups, ee > 1)

sim <- ewe_ecosim(m, years = 30, effort = c("Bait Trawl" = 0.5))
head(ewe_wide(sim$groups, "biomass"))      # time x group
ewe_close(m)

The package starts the EwE engine (ewe-engine serve) as a child process and speaks the same JSON protocol as the Python SDK, so both return the same numbers.

Install the package and an engine bundle as described in Install. Requires jsonlite and processx; charts need ggplot2.

docs.title: Network analysis and ecological indicators
docs.text:
m <- ewe_library_load("anchovy-bay")
na <- ewe_network_analysis(m)              # EwE's Network Analysis plug-in, on the Ecopath model
na$summary                                 # throughput, Finn's cycling index, ascendency, TE, ...
ewe_mti_matrix(na)                         # mixed trophic impacts (rows impact columns)
head(ewe_ecosim_network_analysis(m, years = 20)$indices)   # network indices per time step

ind <- ewe_indicators(m, ecosim = TRUE)    # Ecological Indicators plug-in
ind$ecopath                                # indicator, category, value
head(ind$ecosim)                           # time step x indicator

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
With ggplot2 installed (install.packages("ggplot2"); it is in Suggests), ewe_plot_*() functions return ggplot objects, so they print as charts and take more layers with +:

sim <- ewe_ecosim(m)
ewe_plot_ecosim(sim, relative = TRUE)                # small multiples past eight groups
ewe_plot_ecosim(sim, "catch", groups = c("Cod", "Anchovy"))
ewe_plot_fleets(sim)                                 # landings by fleet, stacked
ewe_plot_compare(list(baseline = sim, "seiners x2" = ewe_ecosim(m, effort = c(Seiners = 2))))
ewe_plot_fit(ewe_time_series(m, 2), list(before = sim, after = after))
ewe_plot_fit_iterations(fit)
ewe_plot_monte_carlo(ewe_monte_carlo(m, trials = 50))
ewe_plot_mse(ewe_mse(m), "catch")
ewe_plot_msy(ewe_msy(m, "Anchovy")); ewe_plot_fmsy(ewe_fmsy(m))
ewe_plot_ecospace_map(sp, "Cod"); ewe_plot_ecospace_map(sp); ewe_plot_ecospace(sp)
ewe_plot_foodweb(m); ewe_plot_trophic_levels(ewe_ecopath(m))
ewe_plot_mti(ewe_network_analysis(m))
ewe_plot_theme("dark")                               # dark palette for every chart after this

docs.title: Building and editing models
docs.text:
doc <- ewe_new_model("Toy bay", area = 100)
doc <- ewe_add_group(doc, "Fish", biomass_area = 2, pb = 0.8, qb = 4)
doc <- ewe_add_group(doc, "Zooplankton", pb = 30, qb = 100, ee = 0.9)
doc <- ewe_add_group(doc, "Phytoplankton", "producer", biomass_area = 15, pb = 120)
doc <- ewe_add_group(doc, "Detritus", "detritus", biomass_area = 50)
doc <- ewe_set_diet(doc, "Fish", c(Zooplankton = 1))
doc <- ewe_set_diet(doc, "Zooplankton", c(Phytoplankton = 0.8, Detritus = 0.2))
doc <- ewe_add_fleet(doc, "Trawl")
doc <- ewe_set_catch(doc, "Trawl", "Fish", landings = 0.3)
doc <- ewe_add_ecosim_scenario(doc, "Baseline", years = 20)
ewe_validate(doc)
ewe_save_model(doc, "toy.eiixml")

m <- ewe_open("Tampa_Bay.eiixml")
doc <- ewe_document(m)
doc <- ewe_set_group(doc, "Pin Fish", pb = 2.5)
doc <- ewe_remove_group(doc, "Catfish")
ewe_apply(m, doc)        # run the edit; the file is untouched
ewe_ecopath(m)
ewe_save(m, "Tampa_Bay_edited.eiixml")

NA means "not entered". ewe_doc_table(doc, "groups") and ewe_diet_matrix(doc) give data.frames; ewe_update_groups, ewe_set_diet_matrix and ewe_set_catch_table take them back. Invalid documents signal an ewe_validation_error carrying an errors data.frame.

Multi-stanza groups, Ecosim inputs and time series to fit to:

doc <- ewe_add_stanza(doc, "Herring", data.frame(group = c("Herring juvenile", "Herring adult"),
                                                 age_start = c(0, 24), mortality = c(1.5, 0.7)))
doc <- ewe_calculate_stanzas(doc)$doc   # B and Q/B of the non-leading stages
doc <- ewe_set_effort(doc, "Baseline", "Trawl", c(1, 1, 2))   # per year, relative to Ecopath effort
doc <- ewe_set_vulnerabilities(doc, "Baseline", data.frame(predator = "Fish", prey = "Zooplankton", vulnerability = 3))
doc <- ewe_add_time_series(doc, "Survey", "Fish index", "biomass_relative", c(2, NA, 1.8), group = "Fish")

The Python guide explains the fields; the rules are the same. ewe_fit() starts from the scenario's own vulnerabilities (reset_vulnerabilities = TRUE starts from 2). ewe_from_ewemdb() and ewe_to_ewemdb() refuse to replace an existing file unless overwrite = TRUE.

docs.title: ewe_fit
docs.text:
ewe_fit(m, dataset, scenario = NULL, vulnerabilities = TRUE, anomaly_spline_points = 0L, anomaly_shape = NULL, reset_vulnerabilities = FALSE, max_iterations = NULL)

Fit Ecosim to a time series dataset Runs EwE's "Fit to time series" search. Nothing is stored in the model; keep the result with ewe_fit_save() or ewe_fit_apply().

Argument dataset Time series dataset, 1-based index or name. vulnerabilities Search vulnerabilities, one block per predator with reference data. anomaly_spline_points Also search a primary production anomaly with this many spline points (1 = one value per year). anomaly_shape Forcing function (1-based index or title) to hold the anomaly. By default a new one titled "PP anomaly (fit)", or the existing one with that title. It is applied to the production rate of every producer. reset_vulnerabilities Start from EwE's default vulnerability (2), like the desktop app's "Use default v" option. Off by default, so the search refines the scenario's own vulnerabilities. The result keeps the best parameters the search tried, and messages warns when the fit still scores worse than the scenario as stored. max_iterations Stop the search early.

Returns: A list: ss_before, ss_after (with the fitted values, as the scenario runs once saved), aic, iterations, vulnerabilities (before/after per link) and, with an anomaly search, anomaly_shape and anomaly (month, year, value).

docs.title: ewe_fit_save
docs.text:
ewe_fit_save(m, fit, path, reopen = TRUE, only_changed = FALSE)

Keep a fit: save it with the model, or load it into the session ewe_fit_save() writes the model as .eiixml with the fitted vulnerabilities and anomaly stored in the fit's scenario, where the EwE desktop app keeps them. The anomaly is a forcing function applied to the production rate of every producer; forcing functions are shared by all scenarios of a model. The session continues on the saved file unless reopen = FALSE. ewe_fit_apply() loads the fitted values into the session so later runs use them, without writing the original file.

Argument fit The result of ewe_fit(). only_changed Write only the links the search changed (by default all links, since reset_vulnerabilities also changes links outside the searched blocks).

Returns: ewe_fit_save(): the path written, invisibly. ewe_fit_apply(): a list with vulnerabilities_written and anomaly_shape, invisibly.

docs.title: ewe_msy
docs.text:
ewe_msy(m, target = NULL, mode = "group", scenario = NULL, max_rel_f = NULL, steps = NULL, trial_years = NULL, to_depletion = FALSE)

Equilibrium yield curves (MSY) Varies the F of one group (or the effort of one or all fleets) and runs Ecosim to equilibrium at each step, under full compensation and a stationary system.

Argument target Group (group mode) or fleet (fleet mode; NULL for all fleets), by name or index. mode "group" or "fleet". max_rel_f Highest F as a multiple of the target's base F (group mode), or highest effort multiplier. steps Number of equal F steps between 0 and the highest F. trial_years Years Ecosim runs at each F. to_depletion Keep raising F until the catch is depleted.

docs.text:
ewe_policy_search(m, scenario = NULL, years = NULL, weights = NULL, parameters = NULL, groups = NULL, fleets = NULL, blocks = NULL, max_evaluations = NULL)

Fishing policy search Searches fleet effort multipliers that maximise a weighted objective (net economic value, social, mandated rebuilding, ecosystem structure, biodiversity).

Argument weights Named list of objective weights, e.g. list(economic_weight = 1, ecosystem_weight = 0.5). parameters Named list of search parameters, e.g. n_runs, init_option, discount_rate. groups,fleets Named lists of per-group / per-fleet objective settings. blocks Named list: fleet to one block code for all years, or one code per year. Fleets sharing a code share one multiplier; 0 leaves a fleet out. max_evaluations Cap on objective evaluations.

Returns: A list: result (objective and its parts), blocks and effort (multipliers found), fleets, progress, and the settings used.

docs.title: Engine CLI and protocol
docs.text:
The Python and R packages are thin clients of ewe-engine, a small program that wraps EwE's computational core. Other languages and tools can use it directly.

A small, stable facade over cCore for use from other languages and from the command line. It is new C# code on top of EwECore and leaves the maths untouched.

ewe-engine run model.eiixml [--scenario N|NAME] [--years N] [--effort FLEET=MULT ...] [--out DIR]
ewe-engine info model.eiixml
ewe-engine serve                 # JSON lines over stdin/stdout (used by the Python and R SDKs)

Build with dotnet build Sources/EwEEngine -c Release on Windows, macOS or Linux. Off Windows the net48 target of EwEUtils/EwECore is skipped automatically (Sources/Directory.Build.targets); on Windows pass -p:EwENet10Only=true to do the same.

docs.title: Protocol (version 1)
docs.text:
One JSON object per line. Request {"id": 1, "method": "...", "params": {...}}, response {"id": 1, "result": ...} or {"id": 1, "error": {"message": "...", "type": "..."}}. On start the server prints {"ready": {...version...}}; send "shutdown" to stop.

method params result version engine, EwECore, protocol, runtime and OS open path model info: name, sizes, groups, fleets, scenarios tables info same as open ecopath_inputs groups, diet (long), catch (by fleet) tables ecopath balanced, unbalanced_groups, groups table ecosim scenario, years, effort {fleet: multiplier}, vulnerability_multiplier, fleets groups and fleets (long, monthly), summary time_series scenario, dataset datasets table; with dataset, its series (long, yearly) fit scenario, dataset, vulnerabilities, anomaly_spline_points, anomaly_shape, reset_vulnerabilities (default false), max_iterations ss_before, ss_after (fresh reload with the fitted values), search_ss, aic, iterations, vulnerabilities (before/after per feeding link); with an anomaly search anomaly_shape and anomaly (month, year, value) fit_save fit {scenario, vulnerabilities [{predator, prey, vulnerability}], anomaly {shape, values}}, path, base, open writes the fit into the scenario; vulnerabilities_written, anomaly_shape, path, info if reopened fit_apply fit, base reloads the session with the fit applied (scratch file); info monte_carlo scenario, trials, seed, years, dataset trials (sum of squares), inputs (sampled Ecopath inputs), biomass (start/end per trial and group) ecotracer scenario, tracer_scenario, years concentrations (long, monthly; group (environment) is the environment) ecospace scenario, space_scenario, years, maps grid size, groups (map totals per time step), biomass_maps {group: rows x cols, null on land} mse scenario, trials, seed, years, parameters, groups, fleets, trial_values settings used, groups/fleets (biomass, catch, effort statistics over trials), value, yearly (mean and 5/50/95% per year), trial_values msy scenario, mode (group/fleet), target, max_rel_f, steps, trial_years, to_depletion curve (equilibrium biomass/catch per F, both assessments), optimum, baseline fmsy scenario, max_rel_f, steps, trial_years groups (FMSY, MSY, value per fished group and assessment) policy_search scenario, years, weights, parameters, groups, fleets, blocks, max_evaluations result (objective and its parts), blocks/effort (multipliers found), fleets, progress network_analysis summary (indicator, value, unit), ascendency (by source), groups (ascendency terms, keystoneness, PPR, L index, Psust), trophic_levels, decomposition, mixed_trophic_impacts (long) ecosim_network_analysis scenario, years, ppr indices: network indices per Ecosim time step (with ppr, also PPR, L index, Psust) indicators ecosim, scenario, years catalog, ecopath (indicator, category, value); with ecosim, ecosim (time step x indicator) model_export path (default: the open model) the model as a JSON model document model_validate model valid, errors, warnings (each {path, message}) model_save model (optional), path, base (file or "template"; default the open model), open path, warnings, info if reopened model_apply model, base reloads the session on the edited model (scratch file); info, warnings model_schema JSON Schema of model documents close true

Tables are columnar: {"columns": [...], "data": {"col": [...]}}. Missing values (NaN, EwE's -9999) are null. Groups and fleets are identified by name; index columns are EwE's 1-based indices. Ecosim overrides apply to one call only (the scenario is reloaded on every run), and so do fitted vulnerabilities and Monte Carlo samples until fit_save or fit_apply stores them. fit_save writes vulnerabilities to EcosimScenarioForcingMatrix and the anomaly to a forcing function (EcosimShape/EcosimShapeTime, default title "PP anomaly (fit)", updated in place when it exists) applied as a production rate multiplier to every producer (EcosimScenarioPredPreyShape). An anomaly search without anomaly_shape uses that shape, or adds it in memory for the run, since the .eiixml data source cannot add shapes itself.

The management calls take EwE's own settings by name in snake_case (parameters, and groups / fleets keyed by name or 1-based index), for example {"parameters": {"regulatory_mode": "NoRegulations"}, "groups": {"Cod": {"fixed_f": 0.2}}}. Case and underscores are ignored, enum values go by name, an unknown name lists the known ones, and a value EwE's validation refuses is an error. Results echo the settings used, and every override is put back after the call.

The module, management and analysis calls (time_series to indicators) also return messages: what the core reported while running, such as Ecospace warning about groups with too little habitat. In the desktop app these are pop-ups; headless, the core answers its own questions with the default and carries on, so check them when results look odd. Set EWE_ENGINE_LOG=1 to echo them to stderr as they happen.

docs.title: Network analysis and ecological indicators
docs.text: network_analysis, ecosim_network_analysis and indicators run the calculations of the Network Analysis and Ecological Indicators plug-ins (Sources/EwECustomPlugins). Those plug-ins are Windows Forms projects, so Sources/EwEEngine.NetworkAnalysis and Sources/EwEEngine.Indicators compile their calculation files (as links, unchanged) into plain .NET 10 libraries, with small shims for the status bar and user settings they touch. Settings keep the plug-ins' defaults; the optional cycle and pathway listing of the network analysis stays off. Every call reruns Ecopath, and the Ecosim variants reload and run the scenario like ecosim does. The Ecosim network analysis computes its indices at the end of every time step, as the plug-in does when "run with Ecosim" is on.

docs.title: Model documents (building and editing models)
docs.text:
A model document ("format": "ewe-model", "version": 1) is the Ecopath part of a model as JSON: model metadata, groups, diet, detritus_fate, fleets, catch, discard_fate, stanzas and ecosim_scenarios, all keyed by name. The schema is in schema/ewe-model.schema.json (generated from ModelDocument.cs; ewe-engine schema regenerates it); ModelValidator adds the cross-checks (references, diet and fate sums, what Ecopath can estimate). Invalid documents fail with error type ModelValidationError and an errors list.

Saving writes .eiixml onto a base file: the model the document came from (its Ecosim, Ecospace, Ecotracer, time series and other data are kept; rows the document does not touch are written back byte for byte) or Resources/template.eiixml, an empty model generated from EwECore/Resources/EwE6.mdb by python/tools/make_template.py together with column-defaults.json (the Access default of every column, used to fill new rows). Adding and removing groups, fleets and scenarios repeats cDBDataSource's bookkeeping (Ecosim and Ecospace copies of groups and fleets, fishing mortality shapes, cascading deletes). A field left out of an existing group keeps its stored value; JSON null means "not entered".

CLI: ewe-engine export model.eiixml > doc.json, ewe-engine save doc.json out.eiixml [--base model.eiixml].

Dispatcher.Handle(string) is the same entry point for in-process hosts such as pythonnet.

docs.title: Notes from bringing the engine to macOS and Linux
docs.text:
• EwECore/EwEUtils build for net10.0 unchanged. Only the net48 target needed skipping off Windows.
  • cCore is not safe to construct concurrently within one process (a shared variable registry raises "Variable Index already registered"). Use one process per model for parallel runs.
  • lp_solve (MSE effort regulation) ships natives only for Windows and Linux x64. cLPSolverFactory falls back to the managed cManagedLPSolver elsewhere (EWE_LPSOLVER=managed forces it). Contract tests run against both solvers; a randomized cross-check compares them wherever native lp_solve loads.
  • WinForms in core is dead code only (#If 0, comments, an already-excluded file).
  • Ecospace, Monte Carlo, fit to time series and Ecotracer run unchanged on macOS and Linux (tested on macOS arm64 and Alpine Linux arm64/x64). The desktop app drives them through WinForms sync objects; the engine passes none (fit) or an inline ISynchronizeInvoke (Monte Carlo) and runs them on the calling thread.
  • MSE, MSY / FMSY and the fishing policy search run unchanged too. Their managers call the plug-in manager unguarded, so the engine's core gets an empty cPluginManager. MSE had no way to seed its trials and its quota calculator kept the random generator from construction, so even batch runs (fixed seed 42) did not repeat; cMSEDataStructures.RandomSeed and a quota calculator rebuilt per run fix both. MSY refuses to run while reference time series are enabled (the desktop app asks), so the engine switches them off for the run.
  • The .eiixml reader ignored Ecotracer scenarios ("not supported yet"), so Ecotracer could not run off Windows. It now reads them (read-only, like the rest of that data source). No shipped model has an Ecotracer scenario; python/tools/add_ecotracer_scenario.py builds the test fixture Sources/EwEEngine.Tests/TestData/anchovy-bay-ecotracer.eiixml.
  • Access .ewemdb reading uses OleDb (Windows only). python/src/ewe/convert.py converts them to .eiixml with mdbtools on any OS.

Nothing is stored in the model; pass the result to :meth:save_fit or :meth:apply_fit to keep it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default dataset int | str

required scenario int | str | None

Ecosim scenario; defaults to the first.

None vulnerabilities bool

search vulnerabilities, one block per predator with reference data.

True anomaly_spline_points int

also search a primary production anomaly with this many spline points (1 = one value per year).

0 anomaly_shape int | str | None

forcing function (1-based index or title) to hold the anomaly. By default a new one titled "PP anomaly (fit)" is used, or the existing one with that title. The shape is applied to the production rate of every producer.

None reset_vulnerabilities bool

start from EwE's default vulnerability (2), like the desktop app's "Use default v" option. Off by default, so the search refines the scenario's own vulnerabilities; on a model that was fitted before, a reset usually ends worse than it began.

False

The result keeps the best parameters the search tried (its last trial is sometimes worse). messages warns when the fit still scores worse than the scenario as stored. max_iterations: stop the search early.

docs.title: ewe.authoring
docs.text:
Build and edit EwE models: the JSON model document.

A :class:ModelDocument holds the Ecopath part of a model (groups, diet, fleets, catch, detritus and discard fates, multi-stanza groups) as plain data, keyed by name. Edit it with the methods below or with the DataFrame views, then save it as .eiixml, or open it in the engine to run Ecopath and Ecosim. The document format is described by the JSON Schema that ewe.model_schema() returns; the engine checks every document before writing it.

doc = ewe.new_model("Toy bay", area=100) doc.add_group("Phytoplankton", "producer", biomass_area=15, pb=120) doc.add_group("Zooplankton", pb=30, qb=100, ee=0.9) doc.add_group("Detritus", "detritus", biomass_area=50) doc.set_diet("Zooplankton", {"Phytoplankton": 0.8, "Detritus": 0.2}) doc.save("toy.eiixml")

Editing an existing model keeps everything the document does not cover (Ecosim, Ecospace and Ecotracer scenarios, time series, pedigree, ...):

m = ewe.open("Tampa_Bay.eiixml") doc = m.document() doc.set_group("Pinfish", pb=2.5) m.apply(doc) # the open model now runs with the edit m.save("Tampa_Bay_edited.eiixml")

docs.title: ewe.convert
docs.text:
Convert EwE models between Access databases (.ewemdb / .mdb) and .eiixml without Windows.

Two backends:

  • ewe-access (Sources/EwEAccess): Jackcess compiled to .NET with IKVM. Reads and writes Access databases; used automatically when it is built or bundled.
  • mdbtools: read-only fallback for :func:mdb_to_eiixml.

EwE's .eiixml format is a plain dump of the Access tables (see cEIIXMLDataSource.SaveFromDB in EwECore): one per table and one comma-separated per record. Writing that same format from mdbtools (https://github.com/mdbtools/mdbtools) gives a model that loads on any OS.

Requires the mdbtools command line tools (brew install mdbtools / apt install mdbtools).

docs.title: ewe.plot
docs.text:
Plots of SDK results with matplotlib (pip install ewe[plot]).

Every result has a plot accessor, so the usual charts are one call away::

sim = m.ecosim()
sim.plot()                          # biomass over time, one line per group
sim.plot.biomass(relative=True)     # relative to the first year
sim.plot.catch(groups=["Cod", "Anchovy"])
sim.plot.fleets()                   # landings by fleet, stacked
m.time_series(2).plot.fit(sim)      # observed vs predicted
m.msy("Anchovy").plot()             # yield curve
m.ecospace().plot.map("Cod")
m.plot.foodweb()                    # Ecopath flow diagram by trophic level

The functions behind the accessors live here too (ewe.plot.ecosim(sim), ewe.plot.compare(...)) and take the same arguments. Each returns the matplotlib Axes it drew on, or an array of Axes when the chart is split into small multiples, so it can be restyled or saved with the usual matplotlib calls. The data behind every chart stays available as DataFrames on the result.

Colours are taken in a fixed order (validated so neighbouring colours stay apart for colour-blind readers), in the order the series are shown; pass groups= in the same order to keep a group's colour from chart to chart. More than eight series never share one set of axes: the chart becomes small multiples, or the smallest series fold into "Other". set_theme("dark") switches every chart to the dark palette.
